profile.campus: Secaucus / North Bergen, Hudson County, New Jersey (Equinix New York metro campus)
profile.reading:
Equinix's own facility page places this building, NY2, at 275 Hartz Way in Secaucus, New Jersey 07094, with 131,040 square feet of space inside a one story, steel frame structure. The published specifications describe N+1 power redundancy, N+1 UPS redundancy, and N+1 cooling redundancy, a minimum cabinet density of 2kVA, 120v/208v power distribution, a floor load capacity of 150 psf on both raised and slab floors, a double interlock pre action fire suppression system, and 24/7 security with biometric access and mantraps. Equinix advertises a 99.9999 percent plus global uptime guarantee for the building, and lists colocation, Internet Exchange peering, Metro Connect, Fiber Connect, Equinix Fabric, and Fabric Cloud Router among the services on offer there. No megawatt capacity figure and no year of construction are published on Equinix's own NY2 page.

NY2 sits inside a cluster of Equinix buildings, NY2, NY3, NY4, NY5, and NY6, addressed within roughly a mile of each other around Secaucus in Hudson County. Data Center Frontier, a trade publication, reported in 2026 that Equinix's broader New York and New Jersey metro area totals nine IBX buildings and about 739,000 square feet of technical space, and it profiled one of those buildings, NY5, in some detail. NY5 was built in 2012 and expanded in 2016 to 20 megawatts of critical power capacity, fed by four utility lines and backed by eight 2.5 megawatt generators, with the campus staying online for a full week without grid power during Superstorm Sandy in 2012. That 20 megawatt figure describes NY5 specifically, a separate building from NY2, and Equinix's own NY2 page does not publish a comparable power number for this building. The same article described the wider campus as a hub for financial services matching engines used in stock exchange trading, without specifying whether NY2 itself performs that role. This registry has not found any Secaucus town planning record or NJ Board of Public Utilities filing that names NY2 specifically, so the building level power figure remains an acknowledged gap rather than an assumption.

Equinix, the operator, was founded in 1998 by Al Avery and Jay Adelson and has grown into a global colocation and interconnection company running more than 260 IBX data centers across more than 70 metro areas, converting to a real estate investment trust in 2015. Its buildings function as carrier neutral meeting points where enterprise, financial, and media customers lease cages or cabinets and cross connect directly to network carriers and to cloud on ramps for AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, and IBM Cloud. Hudson County's cluster of Equinix buildings, including this one, sits roughly ten miles from Lower Manhattan, a location shaped by cheaper New Jersey real estate and proximity to the Wall Street financial corridor rather than by any single anchor tenant.
profile.campus_sqft: Published individual square footage for four of the five Secaucus buildings totals 550,057 sq ft (NY2 131,040 + NY3 250,853 + NY4 151,771 + NY6 16,393 per Equinix's own site). NY5's individual square footage is not published by Equinix. The wider 9-site Equinix New York/New Jersey metro area totals roughly 739,000 sq ft of technical space per Data Center Frontier (2026).
profile.capacity_note: N+1 Power redundancy, N+1 Cooling redundancy; no MW power capacity published

reading.body:
NY2 is a 131,040 square foot colocation building in Secaucus, New Jersey, part of a five-building Equinix cluster in Hudson County roughly ten miles from Manhattan. Equinix publishes N+1 redundancy for power and cooling at this site, but does not publish a megawatt capacity figure for NY2 itself. The facility markets colocation, Internet Exchange peering, and cloud on-ramps to AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, and IBM Cloud.

The Secaucus cluster sits inside a broader Equinix New York and New Jersey metro footprint of nine buildings totaling roughly 739,000 square feet. One building in this cluster, NY5, was built in 2012 and expanded in 2016 to 20 megawatts of critical power capacity, backed by four utility lines and eight 2.5 megawatt generators. That 20 megawatt figure belongs to NY5 only. The cluster has historically served as a hub for financial services matching engines used in stock exchange trading, taking advantage of cheaper New Jersey real estate and proximity to the Wall Street corridor.

This building's power capacity is not published, which means its role in New Jersey's AI infrastructure cannot be quantified from available data. New Jersey has 48 mapped data center facilities, of which only five publish megawatt figures totaling 111.3 MW. Without NY2's own capacity figure, this campus cannot be ranked among the state's disclosed capacity, and any calculation of its AI hosting potential would rest on assumptions about density rather than operator specifications.
